step.description: Full House: r4c9 is the last empty cell in row 4, so it must be 8.
Naked Single: r4c1 has only one candidate left, 1.
Hidden Single: 1 fits only in r2c2 within row 2.
Locked Pair: cells r1c1, r2c1 contain only 3/7, removing those digits from the cells they all see.
Locked Triple: cells r8c1, r8c2, r8c3 contain only 1/3/6, removing those digits from the cells they all see.
Locked Candidates (Pointing): in box 4, digit 3 is confined to r5c1, r5c3, so it can be removed from the rest of the row.
Locked Candidates (Claiming): in row 3, digit 6 is confined to box 3, so it can be removed from the rest of the box.
Naked Pair: cells r9c2, r9c7 contain only 2/5, removing those digits from the cells they all see.
Naked Triple: cells r1c8, r5c8, r8c8 contain only 5/6/7, removing those digits from the cells they all see.
Hidden Pair: in row 4, digits 6/8 fit only in r4c3, r4c7, so all other candidates there can be removed.
Hidden Triple: in column 7, digits 2/7/8 fit only in r1c7, r3c7, r5c7, so all other candidates there can be removed.
Naked Quadruple: cells r1c9, r2c9, r3c9, r8c9 contain only 5/6/7/9, removing those digits from the cells they all see.
X-Wing: digit 7 in 2 rows (r3c3, r3c8, r8c3, r8c8) is confined to 2 columns, eliminating 7 elsewhere in them.
Swordfish: digit 9 in 3 columns (r3c1, r5c1, r4c4, r5c4, r3c8, r4c8) is confined to 3 rows, eliminating 9 elsewhere in them.
Jellyfish: digit 3 in 4 rows (r1c4, r1c8, r4c4, r4c7, r7c5, r7c7, r7c8, r8c5, r8c7) is confined to 4 columns, eliminating 3 elsewhere in them.
Remote Pair: the cells r2c3, r2c5, r3c4, r5c5, r6c4 form a chain of 35 pairs; cells seeing both "colors" of the chain lose 3 and 5.

Chute Remote Pair: r4c6 and r5c8 both hold 56 in one chute; 6 appears nowhere in r6c1, r6c2, r6c3, so the chute's third box must place its 6 in a row shared with a pair cell, forcing that cell to 5. One pair cell is therefore 5, so 5 can be removed from cells seeing both pair cells.
BUG+1: removing 3 from r5c6 would leave a bivalue grid with two solutions, so r5c6 must be 3.
Skyscraper: strong links on 4 (r5c3–r8c3 and r5c4–r7c4) are weakly connected, so 4 can be removed from cells seeing both r8c3 and r7c4.
2-String Kite: strong links on 8 (r1c6–r1c8 and r3c4–r7c4) are weakly connected, so 8 can be removed from cells seeing both r1c8 and r7c4.
Turbot Fish: strong links on 2 (r5c7–r9c7 and r7c6–r9c5) are weakly connected, so 2 can be removed from cells seeing both r5c7 and r7c6.
Empty Rectangle: in box 1 digit 5 sits on a row/column cross; with the conjugate pair r1c5, r6c5, 5 can be removed from r6c2.
W-Wing: r3c7 and r9c5 both hold 46; the strong link on 4 (r8c5–r8c7) forces one of them to be 6, removing 6 from cells seeing both.
XY-Wing: pivot r6c3 (17) with pincers r5c2 (13) and r3c3 (73); one pincer must be 3, so 3 is removed from cells seeing both.
XYZ-Wing: pivot r2c5 with pincers r3c6 and r7c5; 4 is removed from cells seeing all three.
WXYZ-Wing: sets r1c4 and r7c4, r8c4, r9c5 share restricted common 1; digit 4 can be removed from cells seeing every 4 of both sets.
Unique Rectangle Type 1: r6c7, r6c9, r9c7, r9c9 would form a deadly pattern on 5/6; r9c9 cannot be 5 or 6.
Unique Rectangle Type 2: to avoid the deadly pattern on 4/7, one of r5c4/r6c4 must be 6, so 6 is removed from cells seeing both.
Unique Rectangle Type 3: the roof extras of r3c4, r3c5, r7c4, r7c5 act as one pseudo-cell and form a locked set with r7c6, clearing those digits from the rest of the unit.
Unique Rectangle Type 4: 5 is locked into r9c4/r9c6; keeping 7 there would force the deadly pattern, so 7 is removed from both.
Unique Rectangle Type 5: one of r2c7, r2c9, r4c7 must be 4 to avoid the deadly pattern, so 4 is removed from cells seeing all of them.
Unique Rectangle Type 6: 6 is confined to the rectangle in both rows; placing it in a roof corner would force the deadly pattern, so 6 is removed from r5c9, r6c6.
Hidden Rectangle: r9c6 holds only 35, and 5 is confined to the rectangle in r6c5's row and column; r6c5 cannot be 3 or the deadly pattern appears.
Avoidable Rectangle Type 1: setting r5c5 to 8 would complete an interchangeable rectangle of solved (non-given) cells, contradicting the puzzle's unique solution.
Extended Rectangle Type 1: r1c4, r1c6, r4c4, r4c6, r9c4, r9c6 would form a deadly 457 loop; r9c4 must take one of its extra candidates.
Finned X-Wing: digit 1 forms a x-wing in 2 columns with fin(s) r1c5; 1 can be removed from cover cells that see all fins.
Sashimi X-Wing: digit 5 forms a x-wing in 2 rows with fin(s) r9c1, r9c2; 5 can be removed from cover cells that see all fins.
Finned Swordfish: digit 8 forms a swordfish in 3 rows with fin(s) r2c6; 8 can be removed from cover cells that see all fins.
Sashimi Swordfish: digit 1 forms a swordfish in 3 rows with fin(s) r6c2; 1 can be removed from cover cells that see all fins.
Finned Jellyfish: digit 7 forms a jellyfish in 4 rows with fin(s) r3c7; 7 can be removed from cover cells that see all fins.
Sashimi Jellyfish: digit 6 forms a jellyfish in 4 columns with fin(s) r3c4, r3c6; 6 can be removed from cover cells that see all fins.
Sue de Coq: r1c4, r1c5, r1c6 (23469) with r1c1 in the line and r2c6 in the box form a locked set; line digits are cleared from the rest of the line, box digits from the rest of the box.

Simple Colors on 1: its conjugate pairs (the solid links) are coloured blue and gold, and either every blue 1 is true or every gold one is. The 1 in r8c6 sees a blue 1 in r9c6 and a gold 1 in r8c3, so it is false either way.

Multi Colors on 5: two conjugate-pair clusters of 5. The purple 5s in r4c9 and r4c6 see each other (the dashed link), so they cannot both be true, and at least one of blue and gold is entirely true. The 5 in r7c2 sees the blue 5 in r8c3 and the gold 5 in r7c6, so it is false either way.

3D Medusa: candidates joined by conjugate pairs and bivalue cells (the solid links) are coloured blue and gold, and either every blue candidate is true or every gold one is. The 5 in r9c7 sees a blue 5 in r9c2 and a gold 5 in r7c8, so it is false either way.
X-Chain on 1: r8c3 → r8c6 → r6c6 → r6c7 → r4c8 → r9c8; one end must be 1, so 1 is removed from cells seeing both ends.
Grouped X-Cycle on 1: a continuous loop through 6 nodes (groups included); along each weak link one side is 1, so 1 falls from outside cells seeing both sides.
XY-Chain: r1c1 → r6c1 → r6c4 → r1c4; whichever way the chain resolves, one end is 4, so 4 is removed from cells seeing both ends.
Nice Loop: the continuous loop 1@r2c5 → 1@r2c8 → 1@r3c9 → 8@r3c9 → 8@r2c7 → 8@r2c5 alternates perfectly; every weak link has exactly one true side, clearing other candidates along it.
Grouped Nice Loop: the continuous loop 7@r4c5 → 7@r4c8 → 3@r4c8 → 3@[r4c4, r4c5] → 3@r5c5 → 7@r5c5 alternates perfectly; every weak link has exactly one true side, clearing candidates along it.
ALS-XZ: sets r7c5, r7c7 and r9c2, r9c9 share restricted common 2; digit 4 can be removed from cells seeing every 4 of both sets.
ALS-XY-Wing: hinge r3c4 links r3c8, r5c8 (via 7) and r7c6, r9c4 (via 9); digit 3 can be removed from cells seeing every 3 of both outer sets.
ALS-XY-Chain: r4c2, r4c7 –9– r1c7 –3– r1c5, r1c6 –9– r7c5; digit 4 falls from cells seeing every 4 of both end sets.
AIC: 8@r1c6 → 4@r1c6 → 4@r5c6 → 2@r5c6 → 2@r5c9 → 2@r1c9; at least one of 8@r1c6 and 2@r1c9 is true, so candidates conflicting with both are removed.
Grouped AIC: 5@r1c1 → 5@r1c8 → 5@r3c9 → 7@r3c9 → 7@[r3c1, r3c3] → 7@r2c1; at least one end is true, so candidates conflicting with both ends are removed.
AIC with ALS: 8@r2c9 → 8@r2c8 → 8@[r7c8, r8c8] → 9@[r7c8, r8c8] → 9@r6c8 → 9@r6c9; at least one end is true, so candidates conflicting with both ends are removed.
Death Blossom: stem r4c8 links each of its candidates to a petal set; whichever digit the stem takes, some petal locks and places 4, so 4 is removed from cells seeing every 4 of all petals.
Fireworks: digits 4/5/7 each must land on one of r6c4 (cross), r6c3 (row wing) or r9c4 (column wing), locking those three cells, so all other candidates there are removed.
Pattern Overlay: of the 18 complete placements possible for digit 7, none uses r4c5.
Digit forcing: whether r1c1 is 8 or not, the forced singles agree on the same conclusions.
Nishio: assuming r1c4 = 4 and following the forced singles leads to a contradiction, so 4 is impossible there.
